chapterTitle: JVM Profiling with JFR and Async-Profiler

beats.headline: Why do your profilers blame the wrong method?
beats.subline: It is called safepoint bias. Your legacy tools are lying to you.
beats.narration: If your profiler shows high CPU in a method that does nothing, you are a victim of safepoint bias. Legacy tools wait for the JVM to pause before checking the stack.

beats.title: The Safepoint Trap
beats.subtitle: How legacy samplers miss the action

nodes.label: Tight Loop
nodes.detail: Hot CPU work, no safepoint polls

nodes.label: Innocent Method
nodes.detail: Gets blamed for the previous loop

beats.narration: The JVM only allows stack inspection at specific safepoint polls. If your code is burning CPU in a tight loop, the sampler waits for the next poll and incorrectly attributes the cost to whatever method happens to be running there.

beats.title: Legacy vs. Async-Profiler
beats.narration: Async-profiler fixes this by using OS signals to interrupt threads at the exact instruction they are executing. It bypasses JVM safepoints entirely, giving you a crystal-clear view of Java, native, and kernel frames.

beats.title: Running a CPU Profile
beats.caption: Attach to a live PID with zero restarts
beats.narration: Point the profiler at your PID. It attaches dynamically, collects data for your specified duration, and outputs an interactive HTML flame graph that reveals exactly where your CPU cycles are disappearing.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Async-profiler uses OS signals for precision
Attach dynamically to any running PID
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Wall-clock profiling vs. CPU profiling →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle the mystery of low CPU usage but high latency using wall-clock profiling.

beats.headline: Why is your app slow when CPU is low?
beats.subline: Your threads aren't running—they are waiting. Here is how to find the bottleneck.
beats.narration: If your app is slow but CPU utilization is low, you are likely blocked on I/O or locks. A CPU profile will show nothing, but a wall-clock profile will show everything.

beats.title: Wall-Clock vs. Allocation
beats.caption: Find waits and memory churn
beats.narration: Use dash e wall to capture every thread state, including blocked or sleeping ones. Use dash e alloc to track TLAB refills, which is the secret to finding code that floods the Young Generation with short-lived objects.

beats.title: The Hidden Allocation Bug

steps.explanation: Creates a massive byte array every request, even if logging is disabled.
Guard the serialization with the check to stop the memory churn.

beats.narration: This is a classic production killer. Serializing objects to strings before checking log levels churns gigabytes of memory. Allocation profiling highlights this path immediately, even if the objects die milliseconds later.

beats.title: Flame Graph Anatomy
beats.subtitle: Reading the heatmap
beats.narration: Width represents cost, height represents depth. Look for wide, flat plateaus at the top edge—that is where the execution time is actually being spent. Everything below is just the call stack leading to the bottleneck.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Use -e alloc for GC churn issues

beats.narration: You can now spot memory and latency issues. In Part 3, we dive into JDK Flight Recorder for a full-stack view of JVM health.

parts.partTitle: JFR: The JVM Flight Data Recorder

beats.headline: What if you need to see everything at once?
beats.subline: JFR is the black box for your JVM. It records GC, I/O, and locks with 1% overhead.
beats.narration: Async-profiler is a scalpel, but JFR is the black box. It records everything from GC pauses to file I/O and thread states, making it the ultimate tool for production incident analysis.

beats.title: Operating JFR with jcmd
beats.caption: Production-ready recording commands
beats.narration: Use jcmd to control JFR. The profile setting is perfect for incident capture, while the default setting is light enough for continuous, always-on flight recording. Just dump the file when you need to investigate a spike.

beats.title: Custom JFR Events

steps.explanation: Define your custom event with annotations.
Begin and commit the event around your critical business logic.

beats.narration: You can even emit your own JFR events. They are incredibly lightweight and appear right alongside JVM events in Mission Control, allowing you to correlate business logic with system health.

beats.title: JFR Streaming Architecture
beats.subtitle: Real-time monitoring
beats.narration: With RecordingStream, you don't even need to dump files. You can consume JFR events in real-time, enabling custom monitoring dashboards that alert you the moment a GC pause or slow checkout occurs.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: JFR is a low-overhead black box
Custom events bridge business and system
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Continuous Profiling at Scale →
beats.narration: JFR gives you the full picture. In Part 4, we wrap up by looking at continuous profiling to catch issues before they become outages.

beats.headline: What if the bug happens at 3 AM?
beats.subline: Continuous profiling catches regressions before your users do.
beats.narration: Manual profiling is great for known issues, but what about the bugs that happen at 3 AM and disappear by morning? Continuous profiling is your only defense.

beats.title: Continuous Profiling Loop
beats.subtitle: Always-on observability
beats.narration: Agents run continuously, uploading small profile snapshots to a central backend. This allows you to perform retrospective debugging and release verification by comparing flame graphs across different versions.

beats.title: The Power of Diffing
beats.caption: Spotting regressions instantly
beats.narration: Diff flame graphs are the gold standard for release verification. They highlight exactly which methods grew in cost, pointing you to the regression before it ever reaches your users.

beats.title: Manual vs. Continuous
beats.narration: Manual profiling is reactive. Continuous profiling is proactive. By keeping overhead under 1 percent, you gain the ability to travel back in time and see exactly what your JVM was doing during that last spike.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Use diff flame graphs for regressions
